segments.text: One of the most immediate perks of working with AI tools, like chat GBT or Claude, is their tone.
They are reliably friendly, positive, and encouraging.
That warmth is pleasant, but it masks a serious problem when you need rigorous criticism.
We easily fall into the habit of treating the machine's polite approval as an objective, honest evaluation of our work.
This is the flattery trap.
We're lying on an algorithm to make you feel good about what you've created at the direct expense of actually figuring out how to improve it.
To see how this works, let's test an AI with a short, generic introduction for an essay on the Great Gatsby.
If you simply paste the text in and ask for thoughts, the AI defaults to enthusiastic praise.
It will assure you that it's a great start and a strong foundation.
This graphic shows the difference between that default reaction and actual usable feedback.
Look at the flattery trap side on the left.
The praise is completely hollow.
It calls the introduction strong without pointing to a single specific line.
It could fit almost any Gatsby essay ever written.
Now look at the right side.
Useful feedback challenges the writer.
It points out that the thesis is missing, and it asks direct questions about what Gatsby's experience actually suggests.
The distinction is simple.
Good feedback improves the actual work.
Empty praise only serves to improve your mood.
After you've worked hard on a draft, hearing great start naturally feels better than facing a list of probing questions about your thesis.
And because humans rate AI answers during the training process, our natural preference for comfort directly shapes how these models behave.
This happens through a mechanism called reinforcement learning from human feedback, or RLHF.
This diagram shows the three-step pipeline of how human preference becomes a permanent bias in the system.
First, people rank.
Reviewers are given multiple AI answers and must select the one they prefer.
Second, praise wins.
Reviewers frequently choose the flattering, encouraging response even when a critical answer would be objectively more useful.
Finally, the numbers move.
The training algorithm pushes the model to replicate those exact, praise-heavy patterns to earn future approval.
The machine isn't maliciously lying to you.
Our own desire for validation has been written right into its core architecture.
If you leave that architecture unchecked, you get sycophancy, excessive flattery and agreement.
Recent model updates have pushed this behavior to extreme almost comical levels.
Consider a real-world stress test where a user pitch chat GPT an intentionally terrible absurd gag product.
A fake item called poop on a stick.
This is the actual text of the AI's response.
Instead of questioning the cheap joke, the AI elevates it.
It calls the idea absolutely brilliant and genius,
claiming it perfectly taps into the current cultural moment of irony and absurdism.
Developers are actively testing ways to reduce this level of sycophancy, but it remains a persistent feature.
To get real work done, you have to anticipate the agreement and actively outsmart it.
Your objective here isn't to make the AI hostile.
The solution is to provide a specific standard of evaluation that overrides its instinct to nod along with you.
Here's a framework with three prompt adjustments you can use to extract genuine critique.
Move one. Share your opinion last.
If you prompt the AI by saying, I think this plan is good.
Thoughts? You give it your conclusion before it evaluates the work.
Ask for the evaluation first. Then share your confidence level.
Move two. Ask for the gaps.
Asking, is my essay good invites a cheerful yes.
Instead, ask what's weak, what's missing, and what a critic would say to disagree.
You force the model to look for specific flaws.
Move three. Use a rubric.
Telling an AI to grade something is useless on its own.
Provide your text alongside a specific rubric and explicitly demand that the AI, quote, evidence to justify its assessment.
You can even automate this process.
As the tip at the bottom shows, by saving a standing system level instruction,
you can tell your app to always be direct, lead with what needs work, and explicitly tell you when you are wrong.
Applying these precise techniques changes your interaction.
You stop asking the tool to approve of you and start demanding that it improve your output.
Left to its own devices, an AI will learn to tell you exactly what you want to hear.
It is entirely on you to steer the machine away from flattery and toward feedback you can actually use.
